tip: 가 보세요 (ga boseyo) is 'try going' – the -어 보세요 (-eo boseyo) ending turns a command into a friendly 'give it a try', much softer than a bare 'go'.
써 보세요 (sseo boseyo) = try using it. 쓰다 (sseuda) is one verb for both 'write' and 'use' – context decides which; here it's using the app.
-부터 (-buteo) means 'starting with' – not just for times. 여권부터 (yeogwon-buteo) = 'starting with the passport', i.e. the passport comes first.
하고 (hago) is 'and' for nouns only: 수영복하고 모자 (suyeongbok-hago moja) = swimsuit and hat. It can't join sentences – that takes a verb ending.
You stand a plan up in Korean: 계획을 세웠어요 (gyehoegeul sewosseoyo) uses 세우다 (se-uda), 'to stand something up' – buildings and plans take the same verb.
붙다 (butda) literally means 'stick': 서류 전형에 붙었어요 (seoryu jeonhyeong-e buteosseoyo) = you stuck to the screening, so you passed.
떨어지다 (tteoreojida) is literally 'fall': 서류에서 떨어졌어요 (seoryu-eseo tteoreojyeosseoyo) = fell off at the document stage. Failing is falling.
긴장돼요 (ginjang-dwaeyo) is built on 되다 (doeda) 'become' – nerves are something that happens to you in Korean, not something you are.
설명해 주셨어요 (seolmyeonghae jusyeosseoyo) adds 주다 (juda) 'give' to the verb – the explaining was done FOR you, as a favor. Without it, they just explained.
부장님이 (bujangnim-i) is someone you honor, so the verb takes -(으)시- (-si-) inside: 시작하셨어요 (sijakhasyeosseoyo), not plain 시작했어요 (sijakaesseoyo).
-들 (-deul) marks a plural: 동료들 (dongnyodeul) = coworkers. Korean often leaves plurals unmarked – you add it when the many-ness matters.
To someone above you, 'to' is 께 (kke), not 한테 (hante): 부장님께 (bujangnimkke) = to the manager. The particle itself carries the respect.
여쭤봤어요 (yeojjwobwasseoyo) is the humble way to ask someone above you – plain 물어보다 (mureoboda) would feel too casual toward a team leader. It pairs naturally with 께 (kke).
-이나 (-ina) after an amount adds surprise at how much: 세 시간이나 (se sigan-ina) = a whole three hours. Without it, 세 시간 (se sigan) is just neutral fact.
도움이 됐어요 (doumi dwaesseoyo) is literally 'became a help' – helpful things 'become' in Korean with 되다 (doeda), rather than 'being' helpful.
살리다 (sallida) means 'bring to life' – and Korean uses it for putting skills to work: 경력을 살려서 (gyeongnyeogeul sallyeoseo) = bringing your experience to life.
You can't state someone else's inner feeling bare in Korean – it takes -어하다 (-eohada): 아쉬워하셨어요 (aswiwohasyeosseoyo) = showed regret, not a direct 'was sorry'.
좋다 (jota) states your own feeling; for someone else's liking you need 좋아하다 (joahada): 좋아하셨어요 (joahasyeosseoyo) = they showed they were pleased.
Even adjectives honor their subject: 좋으세요 (joeuseyo) uses the honorific -(으)세요 (-(eu)seyo) ending because it describes 팀장님 (timjangnim). Plain 좋아요 (joayo) would drop the respect.
되는 거예요 (doeneun geoyeyo) wraps the verb as 'the thing of becoming' – Korean needs -는 거 (-neun geo) to let a verb sit after 'my goal is', where English uses 'to become'.
실수해도 (silsuhaedo) carries -아/어도 (-a/eodo) = 'even if': 실수해도 괜찮아요 (gwaenchanayo) = it's okay even if you slip up. One ending covers the whole 'even if' clause.
Before a noun, an adjective takes -(으)ㄴ (-(eu)n): 새로운 일 (saeroun il) = new work. The dictionary form 새롭다 (saeropda) can't sit in front of a noun as-is.
일하는 게 (ilhaneun ge) turns 'work' into 'the doing of work' – -는 게 (-neun ge) makes a verb something you can like: 일하는 게 좋아요 (joayo) = I like working.
더 (deo) tacks 'more' onto an amount: 하나 더 (hana deo) = one more. Same pattern for anything extra – 조금 더 (jogeum deo) = a bit more.
얼마 (eolma) usually asks 'how much?', but before 없다 (eopda) it means 'much of anything': 잔액이 얼마 없어요 (janaegi eolma eopseoyo) = the balance is hardly anything.
긁다 (geukda) literally means 'scratch' – Korean pictures card spending as scratching the card: 카드를 긁었어요 (kadeureul geulgeosseoyo) = I swiped my card.
Fees stick on in Korean: 수수료가 붙었어요 (susuryoga buteosseoyo) uses 붙다 (butda) 'stick' – the fee attached itself to the transfer.
정해져 있어요 (jeonghaejyeo isseoyo) uses -아/어 있어요 (-a/eo isseoyo) for a state that was set and stays set – the limit isn't being set now, it already sits there fixed.
-아/어야 해요 (-a/eoya haeyo) means 'have to': 내야 해요 (naeya haeyo) = must pay. Literally 'only if you pay does it work' – obligation built from a condition.
A whole clause can sit before a noun: 이자가 낮은 은행 (ijaga najeun eunhaeng) = 'interest-is-low bank' – Korean front-loads the description English puts after.
-보다 (-boda) marks the compared thing and 더 (deo) spells out 'more': 수입보다 지출이 더 많아요 (suip-boda jichuri deo manayo) = spending exceeds income. 더 is optional but adds punch.
Costs go in, in Korean: 들다 (deulda) 'enter' is the cost verb – 생활비가 많이 들어요 (saenghwalbiga mani deureoyo) = living costs 'go in' a lot, i.e. they're high.
What you become takes 이/가 (i/ga), not an object marker: 습관이 됐어요 (seupgwani dwaesseoyo) = became a habit. With 되다 (doeda), the result acts like a subject.
갚는 거예요 (gamneun geoyeyo) wraps the verb in -는 거 (-neun geo) = 'the act of paying off' – how Korean states a goal: my goal IS the paying-off, a noun-like thing.
유학을 가요 (yuhageul gayo) marks study-abroad with object 을 (eul) – not the destination -에 (-e) you'd expect with 'go'. Study-abroad is what you go, not where.
Korean sees a test: 보다 (boda) 'to see' is the take-an-exam verb – 시험을 봤어요 (siheomeul bwasseoyo) = took (saw) the exam.
Respect runs through the whole phrase: 부모님께 (bumonimkke) uses honorific 'to', and 보여 드렸어요 (boyeo deuryeosseoyo) uses humble 드리다 (deurida) 'give' – showing done upward.
시험에 붙었어요 (siheome buteosseoyo) – note the 에 (e): you stick TO the exam, so passing takes the 'to' particle, not an object marker.
합격할게요 (hapgyeokhalgeyo) ends in -(으)ㄹ게요 (-(eu)lgeyo), a promise made TO your listener – plain future -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (-(eu)l geoyeyo) would just predict, not commit.
Interest is something you have a lot of: 관심이 많아요 (gwansimi manayo) = 'interest is many'. 에 (e) marks its target – 경제 뉴스에 (gyeongje nyuseu-e) = in economic news.
-(으)면 (-(eu)myeon) covers 'whenever', not just 'if': 읽으면 (ilgeumyeon) = when(ever) I read them. Habitual results like getting angry lean on it – no separate 'when' word.
개 (gae) is the all-purpose counter for things, and low counts use native numbers: 다섯 개 (daseot gae) = five (seasons) – Sino 오 개 (o gae) would be wrong here.
된 (doen) after a length of time means 'that has lasted that long': 십 년 된 친구 (sip nyeon doen chingu) = a friend of ten years' standing.
많지 않아요 (manchi anayo) = 'not many' – the long -지 않다 (-ji anta) negation. Short 안 (an) works too: 안 많아요 (an manayo). Same meaning; the long form is a touch more formal.
못 (mot) before a verb means 'can't', not 'don't': 못 사귀어요 (mot sagwieoyo) = can't make (friends). 안 (an) would claim you choose not to.
